blocks.text: Part VI of the Constitution deals with government in the States. Articles 153 to 167 deal with the State executive: the Governor, the Chief Minister, the Council of Ministers and the Advocate General. There is no Vice-Governor (unlike the Vice-President at the Centre).

blocks.title: How he is appointed (Article 155)
items: The President appoints the Governor by a warrant under his hand and seal.
The Governor is not elected by the people, and not elected by an electoral college like the President.
So in a way he is a nominee of the Central government. Appointment of the Governor by the Centre is a unitary feature (a feature that makes the Centre strong over the States).

Hargovind Pant case (1979): the Supreme Court said the Governor's office is NOT employment under the Central government. It is an independent constitutional office, not under the control of the Centre.

blocks.title: Why the Constituent Assembly chose appointment, not election
items: The Draft Constitution had proposed direct election of the Governor by all adult voters.
Direct election does not suit a parliamentary system, where the Governor is only a nominal head.
An elected Governor might clash with the Chief Minister.
An elected Governor would belong to a party and would not be neutral.
Election would cost a lot of money for a nominal post.
Appointment lets the Centre keep some control over the States.
So India dropped the American model (Governor directly elected) and took the Canadian model (Governor of a province appointed by the Centre).

blocks.title: Qualifications (Article 157) and conditions (Article 158)
head: Rule
Detail
rows: Only two: (1) citizen of India; (2) completed 35 years of age. Being a resident of the same State is NOT required.

He must not be a member of Parliament or of a State Legislature (the Houses of the States in the First Schedule). If a member is appointed, his seat becomes vacant on the day he takes office as Governor.
He must not hold any other office of profit (any paid post that gives salary or benefits).
He gets his official residence (Raj Bhavan) without paying rent.
Emoluments (salary), allowances and privileges are fixed by Parliament by law (not by the President).
If he is Governor of two or more States, the States share his salary in the proportion fixed by the President.
His emoluments and allowances cannot be reduced during his term.
In 2018 Parliament raised it from Rs 1.10 lakh to Rs 3.50 lakh per month.

sections.heading: Term and removal (pleasure of the President)

blocks.title: Term (Article 156)
items: The Governor holds office for 5 years from the day he takes charge.

But this 5-year term is subject to the 'pleasure of the President' (Article 156(1)). This means the President can remove him at any time. In practice the President acts on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers.
So the Article 156 wording does NOT mean he cannot be removed before 5 years, and does NOT mean he must leave after 5 years.
He continues in office after 5 years until his successor takes charge. Reason: the State must never be without a Governor.
He can resign at any time by writing to the President.
The President can transfer him to another State for the rest of his term. A Governor whose term has ended can be reappointed in the same or another State.

When something not provided in the Constitution happens (for example, a Governor dies), the President can make arrangements (Article 160). Example: the Chief Justice of the State High Court may be asked to act as Governor for a short time.

blocks.title: Removal
items: The Constitution gives NO grounds for removal and NO impeachment procedure for the Governor.
Only the President can be impeached (for violation of the Constitution). The Governor cannot be impeached.

Surya Narain case (1981): the Supreme Court said the President's pleasure is not justiciable (cannot be questioned in court). So the Governor has no security of tenure (no guarantee that he will complete his term).
1989: the V.P. Singh government asked all Governors (appointed by the Congress government) to resign. 1991: the P.V. Narasimha Rao government changed 14 Governors.

blocks.title: Article 361 (same for President and Governor)
head: Clause
Protection
rows: He is not answerable to any court for using the powers and doing the duties of his office.
This does not stop proper court cases against the Government of India or the State Government. It protects the person, not the government action — the action itself can still be judicially reviewed.
No criminal case can be started or continued against him in any court during his term — even for personal acts.
No court order to arrest or imprison him can be issued during his term.
Civil cases about his personal acts CAN be filed during his term, but only after two months' written notice. They are not permanently barred.

blocks.title: Related immunity often asked with Article 361
items: Members of a State Legislature cannot be sued in any court for anything they say in the House (Article 194; details in the State Legislature card).
The Governor is not answerable to either House of the State Legislature, to either House of Parliament, or to the Council of Ministers.

sections.heading: Position: constitutional head and agent of the Centre

items: The States also have a parliamentary system. So the Governor is a nominal head (head only in name, also called titular or constitutional head). He is the de jure head (head in law).
The real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister — the de facto head (head in practice).

Key Articles for his position: Art 154 (executive power in the Governor), Art 163 (ministers aid and advise him, except in discretion matters), Art 164 (ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly).
Dual role: he is the constitutional head of the State AND the agent (representative) of the Centre.
He has executive, legislative, financial and judicial powers like the President, but NO diplomatic, military or emergency powers.
He unfurls the national flag in the State capital on Republic Day.

Order of precedence: Governor within his own State is No. 4 — after the President, Vice-President and Prime Minister, and ABOVE former Presidents, the Deputy Prime Minister and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.

blocks.title: Sarkaria Commission (1983–88) on the Governor
head: Recommendation
Detail
rows: He should be (1) eminent (well-known) in some walk of life; (2) from outside the State; (3) a detached figure, not closely tied to local politics; (4) not too active in politics, especially in the recent past
A politician of the Centre's ruling party should not be Governor of a State ruled by another party
Consultation with the State Chief Minister should be written into the Constitution by amending Article 155 (not Article 165)
The Prime Minister may consult the Vice-President and the Lok Sabha Speaker — informally, not as a legal duty
The 5-year term should not be disturbed except for extremely compelling reasons (first body to stress a secure 5-year term)
The Governor cannot dismiss a Council of Ministers so long as it commands a majority in the Assembly

(1) Article 356 (President's Rule) to be used only as a last resort. (2) When the President withholds assent to a State bill, the reasons should be told to the State. (3) The Centre should consult the States before making laws on Concurrent List subjects.
blocks.note: Sarkaria did NOT say the Governor must have travelled widely in the State, did NOT want him elected, did NOT want him removed by impeachment, and did NOT want the office abolished.

blocks.title: Punchhi Commission (2007–2010) on the Governor

By a resolution of the State Legislature, on the lines of the President's impeachment
Governor to decide within 6 months whether to give assent or reserve a bill for the President

The practice of Governors acting as Chancellors of universities and holding other statutory posts (posts created by ordinary laws) should be dropped. The Governor should do only the roles the Constitution gives him.

blocks.title: When does the Governor reserve a bill?
items: Compulsory: when the bill would take away High Court powers so as to endanger its constitutional position (second proviso to Art 200).

Optional (as listed by Soli Sorabji): the bill is ultra vires (against the Constitution); opposed to the Directive Principles; against the larger interest of the country; of grave national importance; deals with compulsory acquisition of property under Art 31A.
Practically required for validity in some other cases: a State law taxing water or electricity of Union authorities works only if reserved and assented to by the President — Art 288(2).

A Concurrent List State law that conflicts with an existing Union law prevails in that State only if reserved and assented to by the President — Art 254(2). Parliament can later override it by a new law on the same matter.
Reserving a bill is a constitutional discretion of the Governor and an example of Central control over State legislation.

sections.heading: Discretion, special responsibilities and constitutional position

blocks.title: The basic rule
items: Art 163(1): a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor, except where the Constitution requires him to act in his discretion.
Art 163(2): if a question arises whether a matter is in his discretion, the Governor's decision is final; his act cannot be questioned on the ground that he should or should not have used discretion.
Art 163(3): no court can inquire whether any advice, or what advice, ministers gave the Governor.

Governor vs President: the Constitution allows the Governor to act in discretion at times, but not the President. After the 42nd Amendment (1976) ministers' advice binds the President; there is no such provision for the Governor.
The Governor is not responsible to the Assembly. It is the Council of Ministers that is collectively responsible to the Assembly — Art 164(2).
Parallels for the Union: Art 74 (Council of Ministers aids and advises the President) matches Art 163; Art 78 (Prime Minister's duty to inform the President) matches Art 167.

blocks.title: The 2025 rulings on assent (as of Nov 2026)
head: Ruling
Held
Why it matters
rows: State of Tamil Nadu v Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025) — 2 judges: J.B. Pardiwala, R. Mahadevan

Governor R.N. Ravi's withholding of 10 bills and then reserving them for the President was illegal. He has no 'pocket veto' (keeping a bill pending forever) and no absolute veto: if he withholds assent, he must return the bill. Set deadlines: withhold or reserve on ministers' advice within one month; against ministers' advice within three months; assent to a re-passed bill within one month (he generally cannot reserve it then). President to decide on reserved bills in three months. Using Art 142 (the Supreme Court's power to do complete justice), the Court declared the 10 bills 'deemed assented' (treated as having received assent)
First time courts fixed deadlines for the Governor and President
Presidential Reference opinion (20 November 2025) — 5-judge bench led by CJI B.R. Gavai; reference by President Droupadi Murmu under Art 143 (May 2025, 14 questions)

Governor has three options: assent, reserve for the President, or withhold AND return the bill to the House. He cannot simply withhold and sit on it. In choosing, he has discretion. Courts CANNOT fix deadlines for the Governor or President. No 'deemed assent' — Art 142 cannot be used to take over their role. Courts cannot judge the merits; but for prolonged, unexplained, indefinite inaction they may issue a limited mandamus (order to decide within reasonable time). Art 361 personal immunity (the Governor cannot be made a party in court for his official acts) stays. President need not seek Supreme Court opinion on every reserved bill
Advisory opinion that sets aside the deadlines and deemed assent of the April 2025 ruling

sections.heading: How the Chief Minister is appointed

blocks.title: What the Constitution says and what convention adds
items: Art 164 says only this: the Governor appoints the Chief Minister. The Constitution gives no procedure for choosing him.
By convention (settled practice), the Governor must appoint the leader of the majority party in the Assembly.

If no party has a clear majority (a 'hung' Assembly), the Governor uses his personal judgement. He usually appoints the leader of the largest party or coalition (group of parties) and asks him to win a vote of confidence (a vote in the Assembly showing majority support) within a month.
The main test in a hung Assembly is: who is most likely to command a stable majority – not simply the largest party.
The Governor also uses judgement when a Chief Minister dies suddenly with no clear successor. But usually the ruling party elects a new leader and the Governor must appoint him.
A person need not prove majority before appointment. The Governor can appoint first and then ask for proof on the floor of the House within a reasonable time.
A non-member of the legislature can be Chief Minister for 6 months. If not elected or nominated to either House within that time, he stops being Chief Minister.
The Chief Minister can be from either House. Usually he is from the Assembly, but members of the Legislative Council have also been Chief Ministers.

blocks.title: Sarkaria Commission (1983–88): order of preference in a hung Assembly

steps.step: Single party with absolute majority
steps.detail: Its leader is invited automatically.

steps.step: 1. Pre-poll alliance
steps.detail: Alliance of parties formed before the election.

steps.step: 2. Largest single party
steps.detail: The largest party claims to form the government with the support of others, including independents (members belonging to no party).

steps.step: 3. Post-poll coalition
steps.detail: Parties join together after the election, and all partners take posts in the government.

steps.step: 4. Post-poll alliance
steps.detail: Parties come together after the election; some join the government, while others (including independents) support it from outside without taking posts.

steps.step: Vote of confidence
steps.detail: A Chief Minister without an absolute majority should win a confidence vote in the Assembly within 30 days.

blocks.title: Other commission advice on the Chief Minister
items: Sarkaria: the Governor must see that a government is formed – not try to form one whose policies he likes.
Sarkaria: if members dispute a Chief Minister's majority, the Governor should not decide it himself outside the House. He should have it tested on the floor of the House.
Sarkaria: the Governor cannot dismiss the Council of Ministers while it has a majority in the Assembly.
Sarkaria: the Union should not set up a commission of inquiry (an official probe) against a State minister unless Parliament demands it.

Punchhi Commission: a pre-poll alliance should be treated as ONE party. If it has a majority, its leader is invited. If no one has a majority, the pre-poll alliance with the largest numbers is invited first.
Punchhi Commission: before dismissing a Chief Minister, the Governor should always insist that he prove his majority on the floor of the House within a fixed time.

blocks.title: Oath, term and salary
head: Item
Rule

Not fixed. He holds office during the pleasure of the Governor.

The Governor's 'pleasure' is limited: he cannot dismiss the Chief Minister while the Chief Minister has majority support in the Assembly (S.R. Bommai case (1994)). If the Chief Minister loses the Assembly's confidence, he must resign or the Governor can dismiss him.

Fixed by the State Legislature. He gets the salary of an MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly) plus a sumptuary allowance (allowance for hospitality expenses), a free house, and travel and medical facilities.

blocks.text: Andhra Pradesh (as of Nov 2026): Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, who heads an NDA (National Democratic Alliance) government led by the Telugu Desam Party (TDP), sworn in on 12 June 2024. Deputy Chief Minister: K. Pawan Kalyan (Jana Sena Party).

blocks.title: Article 163 – Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor
head: Clause
Rule
rows: There shall be a Council of Ministers, headed by the Chief Minister, to aid and advise the Governor – except where the Constitution requires the Governor to act in his discretion.

If a question arises whether a matter is within the Governor's discretion (his own judgement), the Governor's decision is final. His action cannot be challenged on the ground that he should or should not have used discretion. So orders made in his discretion are the category NOT open to judicial review (examination by courts).
No court can inquire whether any advice was given by ministers to the Governor, or what that advice was. This protects the confidential relationship between them.

blocks.title: Article 164 – other provisions as to ministers
head: Clause
Rule
rows: Governor appoints the Chief Minister; other ministers are appointed by the Governor on the Chief Minister's advice.
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha must have a minister in charge of tribal welfare. He may also look after welfare of Scheduled Castes, backward classes or any other work.
Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor.
Total ministers, including the Chief Minister, cannot be more than 15% of the total strength of the Assembly, and cannot be fewer than 12 (91st Amendment, 2003).
A legislator disqualified for defection (leaving or changing his party) cannot be appointed minister during the period of disqualification (91st Amendment, 2003).
Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
Governor gives the oaths of office and secrecy to each minister.
A minister who is not a member of the legislature for 6 continuous months stops being a minister at the end of that period.
Salaries and allowances of ministers are fixed by the State Legislature.

The Governor makes rules for the smooth running of government business and for dividing that business among ministers (except matters in his discretion).

Governor is a constitutional head, like the President.

head: Aspect
Collective
Individual
Legal

Governor, who acts on the Chief Minister's advice

blocks.title: Collective responsibility in practice
items: If the Assembly passes a no-confidence motion, ALL ministers resign – including ministers who are members of the Legislative Council.
The Legislative Council cannot remove the ministry. Even in States with two Houses, responsibility is only to the Assembly.

A ministry facing defeat can advise the Governor to dissolve the Assembly and call fresh elections. But the Governor is not bound by the advice of a ministry that has lost the Assembly's confidence; he may see if another government can be formed.
Cabinet decisions bind all ministers, even those who disagreed in the meeting. A minister who cannot defend a decision must resign.

blocks.title: Individual responsibility in practice
items: The Governor removes a minister only on the Chief Minister's advice – not for his own policy disagreement.
If there is disagreement or poor performance, the Chief Minister can ask the minister to resign or advise the Governor to dismiss him.

So the words 'during the pleasure of the Governor' really mean the ministry lasts as long as it has the confidence of the Legislative Assembly; a single minister lasts as long as he has the Chief Minister's confidence.
The Chief Minister himself cannot dismiss a minister; only the Governor can, on his advice.
The Rajamannar Committee (1969, set up by Tamil Nadu) wanted the rule that the State ministry holds office 'during the pleasure of the Governor' to be removed.

blocks.title: Death or resignation

Any other minister resigns or dies: only a vacancy is created; the Chief Minister may or may not fill it.
Formally, the Governor dissolves (ends) the Council of Ministers.

head: In relation to
Powers
rows: He recommends who becomes a minister; allocates and reshuffles portfolios (departments); can ask a minister to resign or advise the Governor to dismiss him; presides over Council meetings; guides all ministers. His resignation or death ends the whole Council.

He is the main channel of communication between the Governor and the Council of Ministers (Art 167). He advises the Governor on appointing the Advocate General, the chairman and members of the State Public Service Commission, and the State Election Commissioner.
He advises the Governor on summoning (calling) and proroguing (ending a session of) the legislature; can recommend dissolution of the Assembly at any time; announces government policy in the House.

He is chairman of the State Planning Board. He becomes vice-chairman of his zonal council by rotation for one year (the Union Home Minister chairs all zonal councils). He is a member of the Inter-State Council and of the NITI Aayog Governing Council. He is also the chief spokesman of the government, crisis manager, party leader and political head of the civil services.

Duty

blocks.title: Chief Minister from the Legislative Council – limits
items: An MLC (member of the Legislative Council) can be appointed minister or Chief Minister.

So a Chief Minister who is an MLC cannot vote in the Presidential election.

sections.heading: Two Houses or one: Art 168, Art 169 and the Councils

blocks.text: Articles 168 to 212 in Part VI of the Constitution deal with the State Legislature. Article 168 says what the legislature is made of. A State may have one House (unicameral) or two Houses (bicameral).

blocks.title: Article 168: what the State Legislature consists of
head: Aspect
State with one House
State with two Houses
rows: Governor, Legislative Council and Legislative Assembly
The Assembly is called the Vidhan Sabha (the lower House, elected by the people)
The Council is called the Vidhan Parishad (the upper House or second chamber, also called the 'house of elders')
Is the Governor a member of a House?
No. He is a part of the legislature but not a member of any House and cannot vote in it
Same: the Governor is part of the legislature but is not a member of either House and cannot vote

blocks.title: The 6 States that have a Legislative Council (as of Nov 2026)
items: Andhra Pradesh (58 members), Telangana (40), Uttar Pradesh (100), Bihar (75), Maharashtra (78), Karnataka (75).
No new Council has been created and none abolished since 2019 (checked on the web, Nov 2026).

Jammu and Kashmir had a Council, but it was abolished by the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 (a law of Parliament reorganising the State). It was NOT abolished through an Art 169 Assembly resolution. J&K had set up its Council under its own separate State Constitution.
Before 2019 there were 7 States with Councils (the 6 above plus J&K). Old question papers that say '7' are out of date; the answer today is 6.
States WITHOUT a Council include Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, Rajasthan, West Bengal and Punjab.

blocks.title: Article 169: how a Council is created or abolished

steps.step: 1. The State Legislative Assembly passes a resolution asking for creation or abolition
steps.detail: It needs a special majority: (a) a majority of the TOTAL membership of the Assembly, AND (b) at least two-thirds of the members PRESENT AND VOTING.

steps.step: 2. Parliament passes a law to create or abolish the Council
steps.detail: Parliament passes it by simple majority, like an ordinary law. Parliament is not bound to pass it.

steps.step: 3. The Council is created or abolished only when Parliament's law comes into force
steps.detail: The Assembly resolution by itself creates or abolishes nothing.

blocks.title: Key points on Article 169
items: Parliament's law under Art 169 is NOT treated as an amendment of the Constitution under Art 368, even though it changes the State's legislature. Article 169 itself says this.
History: the Government of India Act, 1935 first made the legislatures of six of the eleven British provinces bicameral (Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar, Assam and the United Provinces).
No ratification by the States is needed, and the President's or Governor's separate consent is not part of the Art 169 procedure.

Why this provision exists: in the Constituent Assembly, Councils were criticised as not representing the people, delaying laws and costing money. So each State was left free to have or not have a Council, according to its own wish and financial strength.

Parliament passed the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Act, 2005. The Council was constituted again on 30 March 2007 (revived).
The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 divided the State into Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. It fixed the AP Council at not more than 50 members; Telangana got a Council of 40.
The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2015 raised the AP Council from 50 to 58 members.
AP Assembly passed a resolution under Art 169(1) to abolish the Council.
items.detail: The resolution was sent to the Centre, but Parliament never passed an abolition law. So the Council continued to work.

items.what: AP Assembly unanimously passed a resolution withdrawing the 2020 abolition resolution. The Council continues (58 members, as of Nov 2026).

blocks.text: For the Council's (limited) powers over bills and money bills → see Law-making in the States

sections.heading: Legislative Assembly: size, seats and reservation (Art 170, 332, 333)

blocks.title: Article 170: composition of the Assembly
head: Point
Rule
rows: Directly elected by the people on the basis of universal adult franchise (every adult citizen can vote), from territorial constituencies (areas into which the State is divided)
Not more than 500 and not less than 60 members (Art 170(1))
Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim and Goa: minimum 30. Mizoram: 40. Nagaland: 46. (Some Sikkim and Nagaland members are elected indirectly.)
Constituencies are drawn so that, as far as practicable, the ratio of each constituency's population to its seats is the same throughout the State
Total seats and constituency boundaries are to be readjusted after each census, by an authority and in a manner decided by Parliament (Delimitation Commission Acts of 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002)
The 42nd Amendment (1976) froze seat totals at the 1971 level till 2000. The 84th Amendment (2001) extended the freeze till the first census after 2026.
(i) TOTAL seats of each Assembly: 1971 census. (ii) Boundaries of constituencies inside the State: 2001 census (87th Amendment, 2003), without changing the total.

blocks.title: Why AP still has 175 seats and Telangana 119
items: Section 26 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 says seats shall be increased from 175 to 225 (AP) and from 119 to 153 (Telangana).

But section 26 is expressly 'subject to Article 170'. Article 170(3) freezes the total number of seats until the figures of the first census after 2026 are published. So the increase has not been given effect.

blocks.title: Reservation of seats (Art 332) and the former Anglo-Indian nomination (Art 333)
head: Provision
Rule
rows: Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in each Assembly in proportion to their population in the State. Originally for 10 years (till 1960), extended 10 years each time; the 104th Amendment (2019) extended it till 2030.
Who votes in a reserved seat
ALL voters of the constituency vote; only SC (or ST) candidates may contest. An SC or ST person may also contest a general (unreserved) seat.
Art 171 does not reserve any Council seats for SCs or STs.

The Governor could nominate an Anglo-Indian to the Assembly if the community was not adequately represented. The 23rd Amendment (1969) changed 'such number as the Governor thinks appropriate' to 'one member'.

Last extended to 2020 by the 95th Amendment (2009). The 104th Amendment (2019) did not extend it, so it ended on 25 January 2020. Today the Governor nominates NO member to the Assembly. (At the Union level, the President's power to nominate 2 Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha under Art 331 ended the same way.)
Before January 2020 Telangana Assembly had 119 elected members plus 1 nominated Anglo-Indian member. Now only the 119 elected.

blocks.title: Assembly seats (elected) — States and UTs
head: State or UT
Assembly seats
Notes
rows: Largest Assembly; 85 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes
29 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and 7 for Scheduled Tribes; Council has 58 members
19 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and 12 for Scheduled Tribes; Council has 40 members
Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura, Nagaland
In Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, 59 of the 60 seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes
After the 2022 delimitation; 24 more seats in Pakistan-occupied area stay vacant and are not counted

sections.heading: Legislative Council: size and how members are chosen (Art 171)

blocks.title: Size of the Council
head: Point
Rule
rows: Not more than ONE-THIRD of the total members of the Assembly (not one-half)
Why the size is tied to the Assembly
So that the directly elected Assembly always stays dominant

blocks.title: Who chooses Council members (Art 171(3))
head: Category
Share
Who they are
rows: Elected by members of local bodies such as municipalities and district boards (Parliament specifies which local authorities, Art 171(3)(a))
Elected by members of the Assembly, from among persons who are NOT members of the Assembly
Elected by graduates of at least 3 years' standing living in the State
Elected by persons teaching for at least 3 years in the State in institutions not lower than secondary school
Nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service
blocks.note: So five-sixths of the members are indirectly elected and one-sixth are nominated. Elected members are chosen by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (each voter ranks the candidates in order of preference). No member of the Council is directly elected by the people.

blocks.title: Points to remember
items: Worked example: a Council of 60 seats has 20 from local bodies, 20 elected by MLAs, 5 by graduates, 5 by teachers and 10 nominated.
Art 171(2): this scheme is only provisional. Parliament may change it by law, but has not done so yet.
Council strengths: Uttar Pradesh 100, Maharashtra 78, Bihar 75, Karnataka 75, Andhra Pradesh 58, Telangana 40.
AP Council of 58 = 50 elected and 8 nominated.
In 2021 the Bombay High Court (Maharashtra case) said the Governor must decide within a reasonable time on the Cabinet's recommendation of 12 persons for nomination to the Council.

blocks.title: Duration of the two Houses (Art 172)
head: Aspect
Legislative Assembly
Legislative Council
rows: Yes — a permanent body; it is never dissolved (Art 172(2))
5 years, counted from the date APPOINTED FOR ITS FIRST MEETING (not from the result date or the date it is constituted)
Each member has a 6-year term; one-third of members retire every second year
The Governor can dissolve it earlier (on ministers' advice)
Parliament may extend the term by law, one year at a time; the extension cannot go beyond six months after the Emergency ends
Like Rajya Sabha (both are continuing chambers, but the Council is much weaker than its Assembly)

blocks.title: Qualifications (Art 173 and Representation of the People Act, 1951)
head: Qualification
Rule
rows: Must be a citizen of India
Must take an oath or affirmation before a person authorised by the Election Commission (at the time of nomination)

Qualifications prescribed by Parliament. For the Assembly or an elected Council seat: must be a voter in an Assembly constituency of the State. For Governor's nomination to the Council: must live in the State.

blocks.title: Disqualifications (Art 191) and who decides (Art 192)
head: Ground
Detail
rows: Holding an office of profit under the Government of India OR any State Government. Not covered: a minister's post, and any office the State Legislature declares by law as not disqualifying.
Only if a competent court has declared it
Being an undischarged insolvent (a bankrupt not yet cleared)
Not a citizen of India, or has voluntarily taken foreign citizenship, or owes allegiance to a foreign State
Any disqualification under a law of Parliament (e.g. Representation of the People Act, 1951: conviction with 2 years' or more imprisonment, corrupt electoral practices, etc.)
The GOVERNOR decides, and his decision is final. But he must first get the opinion of the Election Commission and act according to it.
The Speaker (Assembly) or the Chairman (Council), not the Governor. This decision is open to judicial review — Kihoto Hollohan case (1992).

blocks.text: Tenth Schedule details → see Anti-defection

blocks.title: Oath, penalty and salary
head: Article
Rule
rows: Before taking his seat, every member (Assembly and Council) takes an oath or affirmation before the Governor or a person appointed by him, in the form given in the Third Schedule. Without it he cannot vote or take part.
Penalty of ₹500 for each day a person sits or votes before taking the oath, or while knowing he is not qualified or is disqualified
Salaries and allowances of members are fixed by the State Legislature by law, and paid from the Consolidated Fund of the State

blocks.title: When a member's seat becomes vacant (Art 190)
head: Case
Rule
rows: A person cannot be a member of both Houses of the same State Legislature. If elected to both, one seat falls vacant as per State law.
Written to the Chairman (Council member) or Speaker (Assembly member). Seat falls vacant only when it is accepted. The presiding officer may reject it if not satisfied it is voluntary and genuine.
The House may declare the seat vacant if the member is absent from all its meetings for 60 days without permission
Election declared void by a court; expelled by the House; elected President or Vice-President (seat vacated on entering that office); appointed Governor

blocks.title: An MLC (member of the Council) can be...
items: a Minister or even the Chief Minister.
But an MLC cannot vote in the Presidential election — only ELECTED MLAs vote there. So a Chief Minister who is an MLC has no vote in it.

blocks.title: Speaker of Assembly vs Chairman of Council
head: Aspect
Speaker and Deputy Speaker (Art 178–181)
Chairman and Deputy Chairman (Art 182–185)
rows: Elected by the Assembly from among its own members
Elected by the Council from among its own members (the Governor does not nominate the Chairman, and is not its ex-officio Chairman)
Speaker writes to the Deputy Speaker; Deputy Speaker writes to the Speaker
Chairman writes to the Deputy Chairman; Deputy Chairman writes to the Chairman
Resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Assembly (a majority of the members the House has at that time, called 'effective majority'), after at least 14 days' notice
He stops being a member of the Assembly
He stops being a member of the Council
The Speaker does NOT vacate office; he continues until just before the first meeting of the new Assembly. This special rule is for the Speaker only, not the Deputy Speaker.
The Governor appoints a member of the Assembly to do the Speaker's duties (Art 180)
The Governor appoints a member of the Council to do the Chairman's duties (Art 184); the Governor himself does not preside
Decides whether a bill is a Money Bill; his decision is final

blocks.title: During a resolution for his own removal (Art 181 and 185)
items: He shall NOT preside, though he may be present.
He may speak and take part in the proceedings.
He may vote in the first instance (like any member) on the resolution, but has NO casting vote if votes are equal.

blocks.title: Other points
items: Normally the presiding officer does not vote in the first instance; he has a casting vote when votes are tied.
The Speaker names a panel of chairmen, and the Council Chairman names a panel of vice-chairmen. A member of this panel presides when both the main officer and the deputy are absent from a sitting.

Art 186: salaries of the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman and Deputy Chairman are fixed by State law; until then, as in the Second Schedule. They are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Art 202(3)(b)), so the House does not vote on them each year.
Art 187: each House has its own secretariat.
AP history: Nallapati Venkataramaiah was the first Speaker of Andhra State (formed 1953). K. Prathibha Bharathi was the first woman Speaker of AP, elected in the 11th Assembly (1999–2004).

blocks.title: Articles on working of the legislature
head: Article
Rule
rows: The Governor summons each House from time to time. The gap between two sessions must not exceed six months. This applies to a functioning House; it is not an election deadline after dissolution.

The Governor may prorogue (end a session of) the Houses and dissolve the Assembly. He acts on the advice of ministers, except where the Constitution allows him discretion. It is the Governor, not the President, who has this power.
The Governor may address the House or Houses and send them messages (about a pending bill or otherwise)
Special address by the Governor at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year

Every minister and the Advocate General may speak and take part in either House and its committees, but can vote only in the House of which he is a member. An MLC minister can speak in the Assembly but cannot vote there.
Decisions by majority of members present and voting. Quorum = 10 members or one-tenth of the House, WHICHEVER IS GREATER (so an Assembly of 60 needs 10, not 6).

Powers and privileges of each House and its members. Art 194(2): no member can be sued in any court for anything said or any vote given in the legislature or its committees. Art 194(4): these privileges also extend to ministers and the Advocate General.
Each House makes its own rules of procedure (no High Court approval needed)

Business is done in the official language(s) of the State, Hindi or English. The presiding officer may allow a member to speak in his mother tongue. English could be dropped after 15 years (1965); for Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura this limit is 25 years; for Arunachal Pradesh, Goa and Mizoram 40 years.

No discussion on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in doing his duties. Unlike Art 121 (Parliament), there is no exception for a removal motion — the State Legislature has no role in removing judges.
Courts cannot question proceedings only on the ground of irregularity of procedure. But courts can still examine illegality or unconstitutionality (Raja Ram Pal case (2007), on the matching Art 122).

blocks.title: Privileges in brief
items: Members cannot be arrested in CIVIL cases during a session and 40 days before and after it (not in criminal cases).
Freedom of speech in the House; freedom from jury service.
The House can publish its proceedings, hold secret sittings, punish for contempt, and courts cannot inquire into its proceedings.
These privileges do NOT extend to the Governor, even though he is part of the legislature.

Matching provisions: Article 105(2) protects what MPs say and how they vote in Parliament; Article 194(2) gives the same protection to State legislators; Article 361A protects newspapers that publish substantially true reports of legislative proceedings.

blocks.text: Governor's legislative powers (assent, ordinance) → see Governor's powers
Collective responsibility of the State Council of Ministers (to the Assembly only) → see Chief Minister & Council of Ministers

items: 6 States have Councils (as of Nov 2026): AP, Telangana, UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka. '7' was correct only before J&K's Council was abolished in 2019.
Article 168 says what the State Legislature consists of. Article 169 deals with creating or abolishing a Council. Article 171 deals with how the Council is composed.

Article 169 needs BOTH: an Assembly resolution passed by special majority AND a law of Parliament passed by simple majority. This law is not an amendment under Article 368, and no ratification by the States is needed.
AP Council: created 1957–58 (functioning from 1958), abolished 1985, revived 2007, abolition resolution January 2020, withdrawn November 2021. Tamil Nadu Council abolished 1986.
Council: maximum one-third of the Assembly's members (not one-half), minimum 40. Assembly: minimum 60, maximum 500.

Council shares: one-third elected by local bodies, one-third elected by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, one-sixth nominated by the Governor. No member of the Council is directly elected by the people.
Minimum age: 25 years for the Assembly, 30 years for the Council. The Council is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every second year.

Questions of disqualification on general grounds are decided by the Governor, who must act on the Election Commission's opinion (Article 192). Questions of disqualification for defection are decided by the Speaker or Chairman (Tenth Schedule).

Union matching figures (Laxmikanth): Lok Sabha maximum 550 (Article 81); Rajya Sabha maximum 250 (Article 80), of which 12 are nominated by the President; minimum age 25 for Lok Sabha and 30 for Rajya Sabha; disqualifications of MPs are in Article 102 (Article 191 for State legislators).

subcards.title: Law-making in the States
subcards.summary: How State bills pass, and why the Assembly always wins over the Council.
at_a_glance: Article 196 to Article 212 (how bills are passed, money matters, rules of procedure)
3 months the first time and 1 month the second time, so 4 months at most (Art 197)
Can be introduced only in the Assembly and only with the Governor's recommendation; the Council can hold it for 14 days at most
None in States (only Parliament has it, Art 108)
Suspensive veto (a veto the Legislature can overcome by passing the bill again)
President's veto on reserved State bills
Absolute veto (the President can refuse even after the State Legislature passes the bill again)

sections.heading: How an ordinary bill becomes law

blocks.title: Basics (Art 196)
items: An ordinary bill can be introduced in either House – the Assembly or the Council (if the State has a Council).
It can be introduced by a minister or by a private member (an MLA or MLC who is not a minister).
In the House where it starts, it passes three stages: first reading, second reading, third reading. The same three stages happen in the second House.
A bill is passed by the State Legislature only when both Houses agree to it (with or without amendments).
In a State with only one House (unicameral), the bill passed by the Assembly goes straight to the Governor.

blocks.title: Council's 4 choices when the Assembly sends it a bill
head: Council does
Result
rows: Bill is passed by both Houses; goes to the Governor
Goes back to the Assembly. If the Assembly accepts the amendments, the bill is passed
Assembly may pass it a second time and send it again
Assembly may pass it a second time and send it again

blocks.title: Bill that starts in the Assembly (Art 197)

steps.step: Assembly passes the bill
steps.detail: Sent to the Council

steps.step: Council rejects it, or makes amendments the Assembly does not accept, or sits on it for 3 months
steps.detail: This is a disagreement between the two Houses

steps.step: Assembly passes the bill a second time
steps.detail: Sent to the Council again

steps.step: Council rejects it again, or makes amendments the Assembly does not accept, or does not pass it within 1 month
steps.detail: The second time, the Council can delay the bill by only 1 more month

steps.step: Bill is 'deemed passed' by both Houses
steps.detail: 'Deemed passed' means treated by law as passed – in the form the Assembly passed it the second time

steps.step: Goes to the Governor for assent

blocks.title: What this means
items: The final power to pass an ordinary bill lies with the Assembly.
The Council can only delay a bill – at most 4 months (3 months the first time, 1 month the second time). It cannot kill an Assembly bill.
There is no joint sitting (both Houses meeting together to vote) in a State Legislature. The Assembly simply passes the bill again and wins.
The Council can still discuss a bill and suggest amendments – but the Assembly decides whether to accept them.

blocks.title: Bill that starts in the Council – the opposite case
head: Aspect
Bill starts in Assembly
Bill starts in Council
rows: If the other House rejects it
Assembly passes it again; bill is deemed passed
The bill ends (it is dead); the Council cannot overrule the Assembly

blocks.title: Rules for a State Money Bill
items: Art 199 defines what a Money Bill is (taxes, borrowing, Consolidated Fund of the State and similar money matters). Art 198 gives its special procedure.
It can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly – never in the Legislative Council.
It can be introduced only on the recommendation (prior permission) of the Governor.
It is a government bill – only a minister can introduce it, not a private member.
The Speaker of the Legislative Assembly finally decides whether a bill is a Money Bill. (Not the Council Chairman, not the Governor.)

steps.step: Assembly passes the Money Bill
steps.detail: Sent to the Council

steps.step: Council cannot reject or amend it
steps.detail: It can only make recommendations (suggestions)

steps.step: Council must return it within 14 days
steps.detail: With or without recommendations

steps.step: Assembly accepts or rejects all or any of the recommendations
steps.detail: Either way, the bill is 'deemed passed' (treated by law as passed) by both Houses. If the Assembly accepts any recommendation, the bill is passed with that change; if it accepts none, the bill is passed in the form the Assembly first passed it

steps.step: If the Council does not return it in 14 days
steps.detail: Bill is deemed passed at the end of 14 days, in the form the Assembly passed it

blocks.title: Money Bill at the assent stage
items: Governor may give assent, withhold assent, or reserve it for the President – but cannot return it to the Legislature for reconsideration.
Normally the Governor gives assent, because the bill was introduced with the Governor's own prior permission in the first place.
If reserved, the President may give or withhold assent – but cannot return it to the State Legislature.
Same as Parliament: the Rajya Sabha also has only 14 days and can only make recommendations on a Money Bill.

blocks.text: Full detail of the Governor's veto and discretion is in the Governor's powers sub-card. The key facts for law-making are below.
see Governor's powers

blocks.title: Governor's 4 choices on a bill (Art 200)
head: Choice
What happens
rows: Bill ends; it does not become an Act (as Laxmikanth puts it). But the Supreme Court's opinion of 20 November 2025 said the Governor cannot simply withhold assent: withholding must go together with returning the bill (not a Money Bill) to the Legislature with comments
Return it for reconsideration (not a Money Bill)
If the Legislature passes it again, with or without changes, the Governor must give assent. So the Governor has only a suspensive veto (a veto that can be overcome)
The President now decides on the bill (Art 201). The Governor has no further role in it

blocks.title: Reservation for the President
items: Reservation is compulsory in one case under Art 200: a bill that takes away so much of the High Court's powers that it endangers the High Court's constitutional position.
Reservation is a constitutional discretion of the Governor – the Governor can decide it without the advice of the Council of Ministers.

Laxmikanth (citing Soli Sorabji, former Attorney-General) says the Governor may also reserve a bill that is: ultra vires (against the Constitution); opposed to the Directive Principles; against the larger interest of the country; of grave national importance; or about compulsory acquisition of property under Art 31A.

blocks.title: Sarkaria Commission's 3 groups of reserved State bills
head: Group
Bills
rows: (a) A bill that endangers the High Court's position (Art 200). (b) A bill taxing water or electricity that comes under Art 288. (c) Bills that must be reserved under Art 360 during a Financial Emergency
2. May be reserved for a specific purpose

(a) Bills reserved so that they are protected from challenge under Art 14 and Art 19: bills on acquisition of estates (Art 31A) and bills giving effect to certain Directive Principles (Art 31C). (b) A Concurrent List bill that conflicts with a Union law – reserved so that it can be valid under Art 254. (c) A bill restricting trade that was introduced without the President's prior sanction required by Art 304
Any other bill the Governor decides to reserve under Art 200

steps.step: The President may give assent, withhold assent, or return the bill to the State Legislature (only if it is not a Money Bill)
If the bill is returned, the State Legislature (one House or both Houses) must reconsider it within 6 months
If passed again, the bill goes back to the President only (not to the Governor)
President is not bound to give assent even now
steps.detail: So the President has an absolute veto over reserved State bills. Compare: when Parliament re-passes a Union bill that the President returned, the President must give assent – that rule does not apply to State bills.

blocks.title: Other points
items: Do not confuse: Art 111 is the President's assent to bills passed by Parliament; Art 200 is the Governor's assent to State bills; Art 201 is State bills reserved for the President.
Sarkaria Commission: when the President withholds assent to a State bill, the reasons should be told to the State government.

Supreme Court opinion on the Presidential Reference (20 November 2025): courts cannot fix time limits for the Governor or President to act on bills, and a bill is not treated as assented ('deemed assent') just because they delay. The Governor has three routes: give assent; reserve the bill for the President; or withhold assent by returning the bill (not a Money Bill) to the Legislature (position as of November 2026). For details, see the Governor's powers sub-card.

blocks.text: The Constitution gives the Centre four ways to control State law-making. This is one reason the Indian federal system leans towards the Centre.

head: Control
Article
rows: Governor can reserve a State bill for the President; the President has an absolute veto over it

A State bill that puts reasonable restrictions on freedom of trade, commerce and movement of goods into or within the State needs the President's previous sanction (prior permission) before it is introduced
Art 304(b) and the proviso (condition) attached to it
During a Financial Emergency, the Centre can direct States to reserve Money Bills and other financial bills for the President
In 3 cases (listed below), the Governor cannot issue an ordinance without the President's instructions

blocks.title: Art 213 – Governor needs the President's instructions before an ordinance in 3 cases
items: If a bill with the same content as the ordinance would have needed the President's previous sanction before introduction.
If the Governor would have thought it necessary to reserve a bill with the same content for the President.
If a State Act with the same content would be invalid without the President's assent.
Laxmikanth calls the ordinance power (Art 213) the most important legislative power of the Governor.
The President, by contrast, needs no one's instructions to issue an ordinance (Art 123); the President's ordinance power is as wide as Parliament's law-making power.

blocks.title: Art 254(2) – Concurrent List bill that conflicts with a Union law
items: If such a State law is reserved for the President and gets the President's assent, it prevails over (overrides) the Union law in that State.
But Parliament can later make a law on the same subject that changes or cancels (repeals) that State law.

blocks.text: Trap: a Rajya Sabha resolution does NOT let a State make laws on a Union List subject. It works the other way: under Art 249, a Rajya Sabha resolution lets Parliament make laws on a State List subject.
see Centre–State relations

blocks.title: Articles at a glance (Part VI)
head: Article
Subject
rows: Limits on the Council's power over bills other than Money Bills
Bills reserved for the President's consideration
Procedure in the Legislature on estimates (demands for grants)
Supplementary, additional or excess grants (extra money asked for after the Budget is passed)
Votes on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants
Rules of procedure – each House makes its own rules for its procedure and conduct of business
The State Legislature may make a law to regulate its procedure for financial business
No discussion in the Legislature on the conduct of High Court and Supreme Court judges
Courts cannot inquire into the proceedings of the Legislature
blocks.note: Related: Art 194 deals with the powers and privileges of the State Legislature and its members (see the State Legislature: organisation sub-card).

blocks.title: Governor's role in State money matters
items: Money Bills can be introduced only with the Governor's prior recommendation.
No demand for a grant can be made except on the Governor's recommendation.
The Governor can make advances from the Contingency Fund of the State for unforeseen expenses.
The Council can only discuss the Budget; it cannot vote on demands for grants. Voting on grants belongs only to the Assembly.
Expenses 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of the State (paid without a vote of the Assembly – for example, High Court judges' salaries) can be discussed but are not voted on.

blocks.title: State funds
head: Fund
Article
Key point
rows: All State revenues and loans go into it; money is taken out only under a law of the State Legislature
Other public money received by the State
For unforeseen expenses; placed at the Governor's disposal and run under a law made by the State Legislature

blocks.title: Art 255 – a missing recommendation is only a matter of procedure
items: If a bill needed the Governor's or President's prior recommendation or sanction and did not get it, the Act is still valid if the Governor or President later gives assent to it.
So assent cures (makes up for) the missing recommendation.

sections.heading: Council vs Assembly, and Council vs Rajya Sabha

blocks.title: Where the Council is equal and unequal to the Assembly
head: Aspect
Equal to Assembly
Not equal (Assembly is stronger)
rows: Can be introduced and passed in either House
In a disagreement, the Assembly wins. The Council can only delay a bill for up to 4 months. A bill that starts in the Council and is rejected by the Assembly dies
Introduced only in the Assembly. The Council cannot amend or reject it and must return it within 14 days. The Speaker decides whether a bill is a Money Bill
The Council can only discuss the Budget; it cannot vote on demands for grants
Both Houses approve ordinances issued by the Governor
Ministers, including the Chief Minister, can be from either House
The Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Assembly. The Council cannot remove the government by a no-confidence motion
Both consider reports of the State Finance Commission, State Public Service Commission and the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)
Council does not vote in the President's election or the election of the State's Rajya Sabha members
The Council has no effective say in ratifying (approving) a constitutional amendment
Parliament can abolish the Council if the Assembly passes a resolution asking for it (Art 169)

blocks.text: So the Council is not even a revising body (a House that can really change bills) like the Rajya Sabha. It is only a dilatory chamber (a House that can only delay) or an advisory body.

blocks.title: Rajya Sabha vs Legislative Council
head: Aspect
Rajya Sabha
Legislative Council
rows: Continuing House (never dissolved; members retire in turns)
Equal to the Lok Sabha. A deadlock (disagreement the two Houses cannot settle) is solved by a joint sitting (Art 108)
Can only delay up to 4 months; no joint sitting
A deadlock arises when the other House takes no action on the bill for
Equal to Lok Sabha except in money matters and control over the government
Weaker than the Assembly in all respects
Represents the States – a federal House
Its members come in mixed ways (elected by different groups, and some nominated); it has no federal role; so it must give way to the directly elected Assembly

blocks.text: see State Legislature: organisation (composition, Art 169 creation and abolition)

items: The Council can delay an ordinary bill for 3 months the first time and 1 month the second time – 4 months in total. Since the Assembly wins in the end, the Council is NOT equal to the Assembly on ordinary bills.
No joint sitting in States. The 6-month joint-sitting rule is for Parliament (Art 108).
Bill started in the Council and rejected by the Assembly: it dies. It is never 'deemed passed'.
Money Bill: only in the Assembly, only with the Governor's recommendation, only by a minister. Council holds it 14 days and cannot reject or amend it.
Speaker of the Assembly certifies a Money Bill – not the Council Chairman.
The Governor has a suspensive veto. The President has an absolute veto over reserved State bills – the President can refuse even a bill that the State Legislature has passed again.
Returned by the President: State Legislature must reconsider within 6 months (Art 201).
Do not mix up the Articles: Art 199 defines a Money Bill; Art 198 gives the Money Bill procedure (including the Council's 14-day limit); Art 208 lets each House make its rules of procedure.
